title: Real-World Contract: Bank Transfer
story: You're building a banking system. Money moves between accounts. A transfer of 500 from account A to account B must be atomic: either both accounts update correctly, or nothing happens. If account A has 300, the transfer must fail — you can't create money out of thin air. With XIOM's contracts AND ownership (borrowing with `&mut`), you can build a transfer that CAN'T go wrong.
why: Combining contracts with mutable borrowing (`&mut`) creates a bulletproof financial transaction — the compiler guarantees that transfers are valid AND that no data races occur.
analogy: A bank transfer with contracts and borrowing is like two armored trucks swapping gold at a secure checkpoint. Truck A (Alice's account) stops at the gate. Truck B (Bob's account) stops on the other side. The guard (`requires: amount > 0 && amount <= from.balance`) checks that Truck A has enough gold before opening the gate. Only ONE truck at a time can be at the gate (`&mut` — exclusive access). The gold moves from A to B while both trucks are secured. After the swap, the guard (`ensures:` and `invariant:`) checks that Truck A still has >= 0 gold. No gold falls off the truck. No gold appears from nowhere. The checkpoint guarantees it.
try_it: Try transferring more than Alice has (e.g., 2000) — the requires should trap. Try transferring a negative amount (e.g., -100) — the requires should trap. Add a third account (charlie) and chain two transfers: alice→bob then bob→charlie. Track the total money in the system before and after all transfers — is it conserved? Add an ensures that verifies conservation: the sum of all balances before and after should be equal. Can you write that contract?
tips: `&mut` means exclusive mutable access — while you have `&mut alice`, no other code can read or write alice
The invariant on Account is checked after the transfer body runs — if `from.balance` went negative (bug), the invariant traps
Use `var` (not `let`) for accounts that will be mutated — `let` creates immutable bindings
common_mistakes: Forgetting `&mut` on the transfer parameters — the function can't modify the accounts without mutable borrows
Deducting AFTER adding — if `from.balance = from.balance - amount` overflows, the invariant would catch it, but it's better to check `amount <= from.balance` first
Not considering the invariant when writing methods — if `transfer` tries to deduct 500 from a 100-balance account without the requires check, the invariant `balance >= 0.0` would trap
